title: Småprate om været — weather small talk
goal: Open a short weather exchange, acknowledge or contrast the observation, ask one follow-up, and close or continue.

objectives.statement: Open a short weather exchange, acknowledge or contrast the observation, ask one follow-up, and close or continue.

spans.value: Weather gives strangers, neighbours, and colleagues an easy reason to begin a short conversation. You do not need an unusual observation or a detailed forecast. A simple comment can open the exchange. The other person can acknowledge it, add a contrast, and ask one small follow-up question. After that, either person can close politely or keep talking.
Nora and Amir live in the same neighbourhood, but they have only spoken once or twice. They meet while waiting for a bus on a cold spring morning.
Det er kaldt i dag.

blocks.translation: It is cold today.

spans.value: Ja, virkelig. Men sola skinner.

blocks.translation: Yes, it really is. But the sun is shining.

spans.value: Heldigvis! Tror du det blir varmere senere?

blocks.translation: Fortunately! Do you think it will get warmer later?

spans.value: Jeg håper det. Det var mye varmere i går.

blocks.translation: I hope so. It was much warmer yesterday.

spans.value: Ja, været skifter fort nå. Skal det regne i ettermiddag?

blocks.translation: Yes, the weather changes quickly now. Is it going to rain this afternoon?

spans.value: Jeg tror ikke det. Men jeg har med paraply, for sikkerhets skyld.

blocks.translation: I don’t think so. But I have an umbrella with me, just in case.

spans.value: Det var lurt. Der kommer bussen. Ha en fin dag!

blocks.translation: That was sensible. Here comes the bus. Have a nice day!

spans.value: Takk, i like måte!

blocks.translation: Thanks, same to you!

spans.value: This conversation is short, but it has a clear shape. Nora opens with an observation. Amir acknowledges it and adds a contrast. Nora asks a follow-up question. They continue for a few turns and then close when the bus arrives.
You can use the same shape in many everyday situations:
Open → acknowledge or contrast → ask one follow-up → close or continue
You do not need to use every possible expression. One natural sentence at each stage is enough.
A weather opening usually comments on something both people can see or feel. Norwegian commonly uses det er for weather descriptions.

no.value: Det er fint vær i dag.

spans.value: You can also open by saying what the weather is doing.

en.value: It is raining a lot today.

spans.value: Words such as i dag, i morges, and endelig make the opening feel connected to the immediate situation.
Both sentences are correct, but i dag makes it clearer that you are commenting on today’s shared experience.
A short opening can also show a reaction.
These are more expressive than a neutral statement. At this stage, however, a simple det er sentence is usually the safest and most useful opening.
Imagine that you and Nora are standing outside the same café. It is raining heavily, and both of you are waiting for the door to open. Make one short weather observation to begin a conversation.

This activity belongs here because the first step is noticing a shared condition and turning it into a natural opening. Use only the immediate café context. A successful response would make the weather clear and sound like something one person could comfortably say to another nearby person.
The simplest response shows that you have heard the opening and share the reaction.
Ja, virkelig works with many kinds of weather comments, so it is useful when you want a natural response without repeating the whole sentence.
Det blåser mye i dag.

blocks.translation: It is very windy today.

spans.value: Ja, virkelig.

blocks.translation: Yes, really.

spans.value: Ja, det er det refers back to a description with det er.
Det er varmt her inne.

blocks.translation: It is warm in here.

spans.value: Ja, det er det.

blocks.translation: Yes, it is.

spans.value: Notice the complete form:
Do not stop at Ja, det er when you mean Yes, it is. Ja, det er can sound unfinished unless another word follows.
Both are complete. The first repeats varmt; the second replaces the description with det.
Dessverre and heldigvis add a small personal reaction.
Det regner igjen.

blocks.translation: It is raining again.

spans.value: Ja, dessverre.

blocks.translation: Yes, unfortunately.

spans.value: Det er sol i dag.

blocks.translation: It is sunny today.

spans.value: Ja, heldigvis!

blocks.translation: Yes, fortunately!

spans.value: You do not always have to agree completely. A weather exchange often develops through ja, men: yes, but.

no.value: Ja, men det er ganske varmt.

en.value: Yes, but it is quite warm.
Yes, but the sun is shining.

no.value: Det er kaldt, men det blåser ikke.

en.value: It is cold, but it is not windy.

no.value: Det regner, men det er ikke kaldt.

en.value: It is raining, but it is not cold.

spans.value: A contrast should connect directly to the first observation.
Det er fint vær i dag.

blocks.translation: The weather is nice today.

spans.value: Ja, men det blåser litt.

blocks.translation: Yes, but it is a little windy.

spans.value: Amir does not reject Nora’s comment. He acknowledges the pleasant weather and adds another detail. This keeps the tone friendly.
Compare the effect:

en.value: Yes, but it is a little windy.

spans.value: The first response directly contradicts the speaker. It may be appropriate if you strongly disagree, but the second is usually smoother for light small talk.

sections.title: Second checkpoint: acknowledge, then add one detail

spans.value: Return to the rainy café. Nora says that it is raining a lot. Respond with a brief acknowledgement and add one contrasting or supporting weather detail from the same scene.

This activity follows the opening because small talk needs a response, not another unrelated statement. A successful response would show that you understood Nora and could connect a second observation with her first one.
A follow-up question shows interest and gives the other person an easy way to continue. Keep it short and connected to the weather already mentioned.
You can ask what the other person expects.

no.value: Tror du det blir varmere senere?

en.value: Do you think it will get warmer later?

no.value: Tror du det slutter å regne snart?

en.value: Do you think it will stop raining soon?
Is it going to rain this afternoon?

spans.value: You can ask about the other person’s reaction or preference.

en.value: Do you like this kind of weather?

no.value: Synes du det er for kaldt?

en.value: Do you think it is too cold?

spans.value: You can also ask a practical question that fits the immediate situation.

no.value: Har du varme klær med deg?

en.value: Do you have warm clothes with you?

spans.value: A good follow-up grows naturally from the opening.
Det regner mye i dag.

blocks.translation: It is raining a lot today.

spans.value: Ja, dessverre. Har du paraply?

blocks.translation: Yes, unfortunately. Do you have an umbrella?

spans.value: The practical question works because both people are outside in the rain.
Det er varmt i dag.

blocks.translation: It is warm today.

spans.value: Ja, virkelig. Tror du det blir like varmt i morgen?

blocks.translation: Yes, really. Do you think it will be just as warm tomorrow?

spans.value: The second sentence continues the same topic without requiring specialist knowledge about the forecast.

Avoid making the follow-up too broad. Hvordan er været? means What is the weather like?, but it sounds unnecessary when both speakers are standing outside and can already see the weather. A more specific question is usually more natural.

no.value: Tror du det begynner å regne?

en.value: Do you think it will start raining?

spans.value: This asks about a possible change and gives the other person something clear to answer.
Weather small talk does not require certainty. You can answer with a brief opinion or hope.
These short answers can be followed by one weather detail.

no.value: Jeg tror det. Det blir nok varmere senere.

en.value: I think so. It will probably get warmer later.

no.value: Jeg tror ikke det. Himmelen er ganske klar.

en.value: I don’t think so. The sky is quite clear.

spans.value: You are not trying to provide an official forecast. You are simply keeping the exchange moving.

sections.title: Third checkpoint: build the middle of the exchange

spans.value: Imagine that Amir comments on the strong wind while you are waiting for a ferry. Acknowledge his observation, add a short contrast, and ask one relevant follow-up question.

This activity combines the middle stages because real small talk often moves from reaction to question in a single turn. The ferry setting gives you a shared outdoor context. A successful response would remain focused on the weather, connect its sentences naturally, and make it easy for Amir to answer.
A weather exchange can end after only two or three turns. A short closing is not rude when the situation changes, someone needs to leave, or there is nothing more to add.

no.value: Vi får håpe det blir bedre.

en.value: We’ll have to hope it gets better.

no.value: Vi får håpe det holder seg tørt.

en.value: We’ll have to hope it stays dry.

no.value: Godt å komme inn i varmen.

en.value: It is good to get inside where it is warm.

spans.value: The closing can refer back to the weather before moving to a polite farewell.
Tror du det slutter å regne snart?

blocks.translation: Do you think it will stop raining soon?

spans.value: Jeg håper det. Vi får håpe det blir bedre. Ha en fin dag!

blocks.translation: I hope so. We’ll have to hope it gets better. Have a nice day!

spans.value: If both people want to continue, add another connected question instead of a farewell.
Det er fint vær i dag.

blocks.translation: The weather is nice today.

spans.value: Ja, endelig! Skal du være ute i ettermiddag?

blocks.translation: Yes, finally! Are you going to be outside this afternoon?

spans.value: The question still grows from the weather observation. It allows the conversation to continue without abruptly changing subject.
Making the opening too formal
Været er fint i dag is grammatically correct, but Det er fint vær i dag often sounds more natural as a casual opening.

no.value: Det er fint vær i dag.

spans.value: The first describes the weather directly. The second is a common conversational way to comment on the day.
Repeating without responding
If one person says it is cold, simply making another separate weather statement can feel disconnected.
Det er kaldt i dag.

blocks.translation: It is cold today.

spans.value: Det regner.

blocks.translation: It is raining.

spans.value: Both statements may be true, but Amir has not clearly acknowledged Nora. A connector makes the relationship clearer.
Ja, og det regner også.

blocks.translation: Yes, and it is raining too.

spans.value: Asking an unrelated question too quickly
A weather opening creates a small shared topic. Stay with it for at least one response.
Det blåser mye i dag.

blocks.translation: It is very windy today.

spans.value: A question about rain, clothing, or tomorrow’s weather would continue naturally. An abrupt question about an unrelated personal matter may make the opening feel unfinished.
Giving too much information

Small talk works well with short turns. A detailed explanation of several days of forecasts can place too much pressure on a new conversation partner. At A1, aim for an acknowledgement, one detail, and one question.

no.value: Ja, virkelig. Men det er ikke kaldt. Tror du det begynner å regne?

en.value: Yes, really. But it is not cold. Do you think it will start raining?

spans.value: This is enough to show attention and invite a reply.
Later that week, Nora and Amir meet again. This time the weather has changed.
Hei! Det er mye varmere i dag.

blocks.translation: Hi! It is much warmer today.

spans.value: Ja, heldigvis. Men det blåser fortsatt litt.

blocks.translation: Yes, fortunately. But it is still a little windy.

spans.value: Det gjør det. Tror du det blir regn senere?

blocks.translation: It does. Do you think it will rain later?

spans.value: Kanskje. Jeg har med paraply i dag.

blocks.translation: Maybe. I have an umbrella with me today.

spans.value: Det var lurt. Vi får håpe det holder seg tørt.

blocks.translation: That was sensible. We’ll have to hope it stays dry.

spans.value: Ja. Der kommer bussen igjen!

blocks.translation: Yes. Here comes the bus again!

spans.value: (Det gjør det means It does and echoes an action verb such as blåser; Ja, det er det means Yes, it is and echoes a description with det er.)

This second exchange reuses the same pattern in a new weather situation. Amir opens. Nora acknowledges and contrasts. Amir asks a follow-up. Nora answers briefly, and Amir moves toward a natural close.

Create a short exchange between Nora and Amir outside a grocery shop on a hot afternoon. One person should open with a weather observation. The other should acknowledge or gently contrast it and ask one related follow-up. End by either closing politely or adding one sentence that clearly continues the exchange.

This activity brings all parts together in a familiar everyday setting. A successful exchange would remain brief, use connected turns, and make the direction of the conversation clear from opening to close or continuation.

Without looking back, produce one weather opening, one natural acknowledgement or contrast, one follow-up question, and one closing sentence. Keep all four lines connected to the same weather situation.
